content:
Purpose: To develop and evaluate a locally deployed multi-agent AI system for radiology report structuring and quality assurance.

Materials and Methods: This retrospective study included 638 radiology reports from CT examinations of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis dictated by 15 board-certified radiologists in 2023 and 2024. The multi-agent AI pipeline consisted of three agents: (1) a structuring agent that segmented reports into standardized anatomical sections at the sentence level using regex rules and local large language models; (2) a consistency-checking agent that detected mismatches between the Findings and Impression sections or within sections; and (3) a QA agent that identified gender-anatomy conflicts and undocumented communication of critical findings using rule-based and language model prompts. The system’s structuring and QA functions were evaluated together as a unified workflow. For radiologist evaluation, a random subset of 45 reports was selected to represent the distribution of body regions and flagged issues in the full dataset. Two board-certified radiologists independently reviewed these reports. “Correctly restructured” was defined as accurate anatomical section assignment without altering original content; “incorrectly restructured” indicated misassignment or loss of information; “disagreement” reflected differing reviewer assessments. Inter-rater agreement was calculated using Cohen’s kappa.

Results: The multi-agent system structured the Findings sections of all reports (22,270 sentences) into a predefined anatomical format while retaining the original report content. The system flagged 90 (14.1%, 95% CI: 11.5–17.0%) reports, most commonly for section mismatches (80 reports, 12.5%, 95% CI: 10.1–15.4%). Gender-anatomy conflicts were detected in 5 reports (0.8%), and undocumented communication of critical findings in 3 reports (0.5%). In the radiologist evaluation, both reviewers agreed that 31 reports (69%, 95% CI: 53–82%) were correctly restructured, 2 reports (4%, 95% CI: 0–13%) were incorrectly restructured, and there was disagreement on 12 reports (27%, 95% CI: 15–42%). Cohen’s kappa for agreement was 0.62, indicating substantial agreement. Both reviewers agreed that no clinically important information was omitted and no fabricated content was introduced. Overall QA performance was rated as "excellent" or "good" in 84% (95% CI: 70–93%) of the evaluated reports, with the remaining reports rated as "fair".

Conclusion: A locally deployed multi-agent AI system combined radiology report structuring and quality assurance within a single workflow, demonstrating favorable performance in radiologist evaluation. Limitations include the retrospective design, single-institution setting, and limited sample size for radiologist evaluation. Such systems may support standardization of reporting and quality assurance in radiology practice.

REVIEW:
"""
- The document would benefit from a clearer explanation of the multi-agent AI pipeline’s architecture and the specific roles of each agent, as this is only briefly mentioned.
- The description of the evaluation process could be more precise: clarify how the 45-report subset was selected and whether this sample is representative of the full dataset.
- The criteria for “correctly restructured,” “incorrectly restructured,” and “disagreement” between reviewers should be defined to improve transparency and reproducibility.
- The reporting of results could be enhanced by providing confidence intervals or statistical measures (e.g., inter-rater agreement) to support the reported percentages.
- The document mentions “gender-anatomy conflicts” and “undocumented communication of critical findings” but does not specify how these were detected or how often they occurred; more detail would improve completeness.
- The conclusion could briefly acknowledge limitations (e.g., retrospective design, single institution, limited sample size for radiologist evaluation) to provide a balanced perspective.
- Consider clarifying whether the system’s structuring and QA functions were evaluated separately or together, as this distinction may affect interpretation of the results.
"""
